Most remote workers on Koh Samui use the Destination Thailand Visa (DTV): it is valid for 5 years, allows stays of up to 180 days per entry, costs 10,000 THB and needs at least 500,000 THB in savings. It lets you work remotely for employers and clients outside Thailand, never for a Thai company or Thai clients. Bophut, Maenam and Lamai are the usual bases, with studio rents of roughly 12,000–28,000 THB a month, fibre in most newer buildings, and a 24-hour coworking space in Chaweng from about 5,900 THB a month; budget 2,000–4,500 THB a month for a scooter and keep a backup SIM.

Not legal or tax advice: visa and tax rules here are summarised as of November 2026. Check visa requirements with the Thai embassy for your country and tax questions with a qualified adviser.

Is Samui good for remote work?

Samui suits remote workers who want a comfortable island base with good infrastructure more than a nomad scene. The honest picture:

  • An international airport with direct flights to Bangkok, Singapore and other Asian hubs, so client trips and visa runs are easy.
  • Private hospitals, big supermarkets, malls and reliable fibre in the main areas.
  • Beaches, boat trips and Koh Phangan and Koh Tao on your doorstep at weekends.
  • A wide choice of monthly rentals, from studios to pool villas.
  • More expensive than Chiang Mai or mainland cities, especially for rent and imported food.
  • A smaller, more spread-out nomad community than Koh Phangan's; you need transport to meet people.
  • Few dedicated coworking spaces; most people work from home or cafés.
  • October to December brings heavy rain, power cuts during storms and occasional slow internet.
  • You realistically need a scooter or car, and the roads are risky.

If you are choosing between islands, Koh Phangan has the bigger community and cheaper rents; Samui has the airport, hospitals and a more grown-up, family-friendly feel. See Samui vs Phangan vs Koh Tao.

Visas for remote workers

Destination Thailand Visa (DTV)

ItemDTV in late 2026
Validity5 years, multiple entry
Stay per entryUp to 180 days, extendable once per entry by 180 days at immigration (1,900 THB)
Fee10,000 THB, or the local-currency equivalent set by each embassy
FundsAt least 500,000 THB, usually shown with 3–6 months of bank statements
Who qualifiesRemote workers, freelancers and business owners working for clients or employers outside Thailand ("workcation"); people on long "soft power" courses such as Muay Thai or Thai cooking; spouses and children of holders
Work allowedRemote work for foreign employers and clients only; no Thai work permit, no Thai employer, no Thai clients
Since 31 August 2026Proof of permanent residence in the country where you apply and a criminal record clearance certificate; applications made in a third country are no longer accepted
How to applyOnline through the Thai e-Visa system, from outside Thailand

The 31 August 2026 change ended the popular practice of applying from Laos, Malaysia or Vietnam during a border run. Requirements such as bank-statement history vary between embassies, so follow the checklist of the mission for your nationality or residence. Holders staying more than 90 days in a row must report their address every 90 days (form TM.47); see the Koh Samui immigration office guide.

Long-Term Resident (LTR)

The LTR is a 10-year visa run by the Board of Investment. Its work-from-Thailand professional category needs an income of at least USD 80,000 a year over the last two years (or USD 40,000–80,000 with a master's degree), a job with a large foreign company, and health insurance of at least USD 50,000. Few freelancers qualify, but employees of big tech and finance firms often do.

Why the 30-day exemption doesn't fit

Since 15 September 2026, most Western nationalities get only 30 days visa-free, extendable once by up to 30 days. Repeated border runs attract questions at immigration, and the visa exemption is meant for tourism, not work. For anything longer than a working holiday of a few weeks, get a DTV. All visa types are compared on our Thailand visa guide, and the legal limits on working are on working on Koh Samui.

Coworking spaces and laptop-friendly cafés

Samui has only a handful of dedicated coworking spaces, and they open and close more often than hotels. We list the ones we could confirm in late 2026 and those that appear in directories but need a check before you go.

The Exchange is reported to be in Maenam. [check]

Khan Space, Be Productive and Mantra Work Lounge were listed in coworking directories, but we could not confirm they still operate in November 2026. [check]

Most nomads on Samui work from home and use cafés for a change of scene. Café working is easiest in Bophut, Chaweng and Lamai; buy something every couple of hours, avoid peak lunch tables, and ask before you plug in. Some resorts sell pool day passes, which can be a pleasant change of scene in the low season.

Internet

  • Fibre: AIS 3BB Fibre3, True Online and the state operator NT sell home fibre plans from about 100 Mbps to 1 Gbps. Newer condos and villas usually have fibre; older houses may have slow or shared lines. Ask the landlord for a speed test video before you sign.
  • Mobile: AIS and True both run 5G in Chaweng, Bophut and the other main areas, with 4G across most of the island. A 30-day tourist SIM with unlimited data costs about 1,199 THB; residents can take monthly postpaid plans.
  • Backup: keep a SIM on the other network for hotspotting. Power cuts are most common during storms from October to December, so a small UPS for your router and a power bank for your laptop are worth having.
  • Speed reality: crowd-sourced tests from Samui average far below advertised speeds, but a good fibre line in a newer building gets close to its rating.

Your first week on Samui

  1. Day 1 Land at Samui airport or by ferry from Surat Thani. Buy a local SIM at an operator shop (passport needed) and check into a short stay in the area you think you want.
  2. Days 2–3 View rentals in person. Test the Wi-Fi, run the air-conditioning, check the water pressure and ask how electricity is billed. Look at the access road in the rain if you can.
  3. Day 3 Rent a scooter on a monthly deal (only if you hold a motorcycle licence and an IDP) or arrange a car; never leave your passport as a deposit.
  4. Day 4 Sign a written contract in English and Thai, photograph the inventory and meters, and make sure the landlord files your TM.30 address notification.
  5. Day 5 Try a coworking day pass and two or three cafés near home; work out your backup plan for power cuts.
  6. Weekend Get out on the water; the island looks different from a boat, and a day at sea is the best reset after a week of calls across time zones.
  7. Week 2 Open a routine: book any 90-day report date in your calendar, find a gym or yoga class, and join local community groups to meet other long-stayers.

Tax residency and foreign income

This is a general outline only; take advice from a tax adviser who knows both Thai tax and your home country.

  • Residency: you become a Thai tax resident if you spend 180 days or more in Thailand in a calendar year, counted cumulatively.
  • Remittance rule: under Revenue Department Order Por. 161/2566, foreign income earned from 1 January 2024 by a Thai tax resident is taxable when it is brought into Thailand, in whatever year it arrives. Income earned before 2024 is outside the rule (Por. 162/2566) if you can document it.
  • Proposed exemption: a plan to exempt foreign income remitted in the same or the following year had not become law as of October 2026.
  • Double tax treaties: most of Thailand's treaties give a credit for tax paid abroad rather than a full exemption, and you usually have to claim it.
  • Under 180 days: many DTV holders split their year to stay below 180 days in Thailand.

Weekends and days off

One of the best things about working from Samui is what you can do on a Saturday:

  • Pig Island and Koh Tan: a half day from Thong Krut, all year. The Pig Island speedboat tour costs 1,450 THB per adult with hotel pickup from most areas of Koh Samui.
  • Ang Thong Marine Park: kayaking, snorkelling and viewpoints; closed 1 November–15 December, reopening 16 December. The Ang Thong speedboat day tour costs 1,800 THB per adult.
  • Koh Phangan: a 20–50 minute ferry ride for beaches and parties; see Koh Samui to Koh Phangan, or charter a private speedboat to Koh Phangan with friends.
  • Koh Tao: snorkelling at Koh Nang Yuan on the Koh Tao day trip (2,200 THB adult).
